analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million at 2%, and above $1 billion at 3%
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place an annual tax on the net worth of the wealthiest American households: 2% on wealth above $50 million, and 3% on wealth above $1 billion. Assets worth $50,000 or less would be exempt, and no household under the $50 million threshold would pay anything. The bill would also direct roughly $100 billion to the IRS over ten years for enforcement, taxpayer services, and computer upgrades, and require annual audits of at least 30% of households subject to the tax.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 99.99% of households with net worth below $50 million would pay nothing directly. If the revenue were later used to fund public services, or simply to reduce borrowing, the broader public would benefit. Stronger IRS enforcement also improves compliance for ordinary taxpayers by making audits of large, complex returns routine.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to net worth above $50 million, leaving every household below that threshold with no liability at all.
The bill authorizes $100 billion in IRS funding from fiscal 2024 through 2034: $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business system modernization.
The IRS would be required to audit at least 30% of taxpayers subject to the wealth tax every year, and penalties up to 50% would apply for large valuation understatements.

The bill strengthens disclosure rules to stop taxpayers from hiding assets in foreign corporations, partnerships, and trusts, and directs the Treasury to leverage data collected under the foreign-account reporting law (FATCA).

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $50 million in net worth — a few thousand American families, concentrated at the very top — would pay an annual tax of 2% on wealth from $50 million to $1 billion and 3% above $1 billion. Owners of illiquid private businesses could defer payment for up to five years, and expatriates to avoid the tax would face a 40% exit tax.

drawbacks.text: Most billionaire wealth sits in private company shares and other assets with no market price, so the Treasury would have to build new valuation rules, and critics note that valuing such assets every year is difficult and contestable.

A tax on unrealized net worth raises unresolved legal questions: some constitutional scholars argue that taxes on property must be apportioned among the states under the Constitution, which could invite years of litigation before the tax collected anything. The provided sources do not address this dispute; it is a widely discussed legal objection to federal wealth taxes.

Even with the bill's deferral option for owners of illiquid enterprises, some wealthy households would face cash-flow strain paying a tax on wealth they have not yet sold, and wealthy taxpayers would spend heavily on valuation and planning to minimize the tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax falls entirely above $50 million of net worth, so the direct cost to ordinary households is zero and the upside is potentially large: revenue from a few thousand of the wealthiest families plus a much better-funded IRS. The real questions are practical, not distributional — annual valuation of private assets is hard, the constitutional question is genuinely unsettled, and enforcement would take years to build. The bill anticipates these problems with deferral, steep penalties, mandated audits, and mandatory Treasury reports every two years, but a serious implementation challenge would remain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on March 21, 2024, joined by seven original cosponsors: six of 48 Senate Democrats and one of four Senate Independents.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill was not carried over, so no chamber ever voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The few thousand households that would have owed the tax — the ultra-wealthy — are better off, since no wealth tax was enacted and IRS enforcement funding did not increase through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The ultra-wealthy, whose wealth stayed untaxed

against.name: Chair Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; the Finance Committee took no action on it after referral.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never left committee, and no Senate action followed beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: All eight original sponsors were Democrats or Independents, and no Republican cosponsored; no roll call ever occurred because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill's entire revenue base is wealth above $50 million, so these households bear the full cost while paying nothing today; their interest in keeping the current system is the direct opposite of the public's interest in the revenue and enforcement the bill would provide.

industries.industry: Wealth management and estate planning services
industries.note: A wealth tax would cut the pool of unrealized wealth that private-bank and planning services exist to shelter, but it would also create a large new market in valuation and compliance work for the very households affected.

industries.industry: Tax-advice and accounting firms serving the ultra-wealthy
industries.note: Annual valuation of hard-to-price assets, new information reporting, and mandated audits of 30% of covered taxpayers would generate substantial paid compliance work for advisers to covered households.
The bill authorizes $100 billion over ten years for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization, strengthening the agency that enforces the tax code everyone else lives under.
